title: DiMaS: Distribution Matching for Steering Vision-Language-Action Models
action_head: flow/diffusion action expert (both models, 10 flow-matching steps)
methods: optimal-transport map (low-rank Sinkhorn) between low- and high-feature tails of action-expert residual representations
linear-probe gate (steer only when feature absent)
linear SVM separability by layer and flow step
baselines: mean-difference, regression steering (Buurmeijer et al.) in VLM and expert, prompt injection
question: Can behavioral features such as speed and vertical displacement of flow-matching VLAs be controlled by intervening on hidden representations, and why does classical linear steering fail there?
key_findings: Linear steering (mean-difference, regression in VLM or action expert) and prompt injection move speed or z-displacement inconsistently; increasing and decreasing versions often shift the feature in the same direction (Figs. 2-3).

DiMaS shifts speed in both directions on both models and z-displacement on pi0.5, with paired t-tests across episodes; speed steering largely preserves success, z-displacement steering costs success (e.g. too low to lift into basket on LIBERO-Object).
Decreasing directions (slower, lower) are more reliably significant than increasing ones; for increasing speed on pi0.5 under cross-suite transfer, p = 0.494 (Spatial) and 0.567 (Goal).

Generalization: steering learned across many tasks (Setting 2) is more consistent than per-task (Setting 1); decreasing speed stays significant on held-out tasks (Setting 3) for pi0.5, and keeps the intended sign but loses significance in cross-suite transfer to LIBERO-Goal (Setting 4).
LIBERO-10 with pi0.5: decreasing speed gives delta mean = -0.024 (p < 0.01, alpha = 0.5) with success 96% -> 90%.

Representation analysis on SmolVLA (LIBERO-Object, speed): action-expert representations are almost 100% linearly separable at later flow steps and > 93% in deeper expert layers even at step 0, versus max 87% in VLM layers; yet shifting along the separating direction does not match the two distributions in PCA ('linearly decodable but not linearly steerable').

Layer matters: on pi0.5, steering at late expert layers (L15-L17) slows the robot as intended, while early and middle layers (L3-L9) push speed the opposite way (App. Fig. A6); alpha above 0.5 trades success for stronger effect.

evidence.scale: OT map fit on about 50 training episodes per suite (~3,500 samples per distribution); held-out initial states / tasks for evaluation; exact number of evaluation episodes per condition not clearly reported in the text read
evidence.statistics: partial: paired t-tests across episodes for feature shifts (threshold p < 0.01), no correction for many comparisons, no CIs or tests on success-rate changes
evidence.baselines: unsteered policy, mean-difference steering, regression steering (VLM and action expert), prompt injection ('go faster/slower')

causal_validation: Yes: interventions on action-expert representations change executed speed and height in closed loop, and a layer sweep shows where the effect lives. The 'not linearly steerable' claim is supported by the failed linear baselines plus a qualitative PCA picture, not by a formal test.
closed_loop: Yes, all steering results are closed-loop LIBERO rollouts.
limitations_stated: Intervention treats all timesteps alike; deciding when to intervene is future work.
For action chunks, pairing each representation with its own action's feature is only an approximation.
Layer choice is model-dependent and not systematically studied.
OT fitting costs about 85 minutes per suite offline.
critique: The features are defined on the policy's own predicted actions, so the method learns to map 'slow-action' representations to 'fast-action' ones; this is effective control but says little about what concept the model represents.
Results are presented mostly as figures with significance shading; success-rate effects lack tests, and the number of evaluation episodes per cell is hard to find.
The finding that early expert layers steer in the opposite direction is important for the field but is shown only for pi0.5 speed.

Simulation only, LIBERO only; no real robot. The 'linear steering fails' claim is shown for flow-matching experts and does not contradict FFN-neuron steering on discrete-token models (Haon et al. 2509.00328), which works through a different mechanism.
Asymmetry (slow/low easier than fast/high) matches the real-robot asymmetry in 2509.00328, suggesting steering can amplify default tendencies more easily than push against them.
one_line: On flow-matching VLAs (SmolVLA, pi0.5), additive steering vectors fail to control speed or height reliably, while an optimal-transport map between low- and high-feature activation distributions in late action-expert layers does, mostly in the slow/low direction.
